explanations: luna: The section’s secondary dictionary form of ف ج ر describes calamities bursting over a people; here فَانفَجَرَتْ is a spring bursting from a struck rock into twelve water sources. The shared root makes a concrete life-giving counter-sense to the section’s disaster image. | terra: Twelve springs burst from the struck stone and each people knows its drinking-place; the exact eruption root is beneficial and orderly here, reversing the source dictionary's many sudden calamities while retaining plurality and distribution.
terra: After giving Moses the Book, God sends messengers in succession after him; this is a repeated formulation of the messenger-by-messenger sequence that the section derives from تَتْرَا.

luna: The verse asks whether people await God’s coming in canopies of cloud with the angels, a specific expected arrival matching the section’s scene; it then warns that the matter will be decided and returned to God. | terra: The rhetorical question asks whether they await only that God come in cloud-shadows and the angels, after which the matter is decided; it is the section's cited expectation becoming an irreversible event.
terra: Every soul finds its good and evil present, مُّحْضَرًا, and wishes a far distance from the evil; presence opposed to desired distance precisely explains what the section says “bringing” does.

terra: A witness is brought from every community and the Prophet is brought as witness against his people; repeated جِئْنَا بِـ turns representative witnesses into persons made present for judgment, as in the section.
terra: Jesus is sent following in the earlier prophets' tracks and confirming the Torah; the verse gives an individual link within the section's larger image of successive messengers.

terra: They ask why an angel was not sent down, but the verse says that sending one would decide the matter and leave no respite; it defines the irreversible boundary implicit in the section's angelic arrival.
terra: People are told that they have come to God فُرَادَىٰ, alone, as first created; this preserves individual accountability inside the section's collective ranks and crowds.

luna: This warning asks whether people await the angels, their Lord, or signs of their Lord to come. It voices the same awaited arrival while its own context stresses that belief after the signs appear will not benefit a soul. | terra: The verse asks whether they await the angels, the Lord, or one of His signs, then says late belief will not benefit; it makes the section's awaited arrival a boundary after which response is too late.

luna: The people of Lot are rained upon, and the verse calls it a rain for the criminals. This is another concrete cascading punishment of a community alongside the section’s dictionary image of calamities bursting upon people.

terra: When the Lord manifests to the mountain He makes it دَكًّا and Moses falls unconscious; the verse tightly joins divine self-disclosure to crushing, while marking how an earthly mountain cannot bear that disclosure.

luna: At Badr God promises a thousand angels “following one another,” مُرْدِفِينَ. Their successive arrival parallels the section’s repeated ranks, while this verse places it in a battle rather than the final gathering. | terra: God reinforces the believers with a thousand angels مُرْدِفِينَ, following one another; this worldly angelic arrival gives a concrete counterpart to rank after rank and to the section's succession motif.

luna: When the command comes, the town is overturned and stones rain down on it. This is a specific sudden, cascading punishment of a people like the section’s secondary dictionary image of disasters bursting upon them.

luna: The earth and heavens are replaced, and all come before God, the One, the Irresistible. This joins the section’s transformed ground to the arrival before the Lord, while depicting a cosmic remaking rather than a flattened surface. | terra: The earth is exchanged for another earth and all emerge before God, the One, the Overpowering; this directly joins transformed ground to universal appearance before the Lord.
terra: The mockers demand, “Bring us the angels,” if the messenger is truthful; this turns the section's solemn arrival into the answer to a taunting request.
terra: The reply says angels descend only with the truth and then people receive no delay; it distinguishes decisive angelic coming from a spectacle supplied on demand.
luna: The town is overturned and stones of baked clay rain down upon its people. This repeats the sudden destructive onslaught described in the section’s secondary dictionary sense of ف ج ر.

terra: God comes at the plotters' building from its foundations so that its roof falls upon them; the effective collapse clarifies that scriptural “coming” can name an unforeseen divine judgment rather than ordinary locomotion.
terra: Angels take the good while saying peace and inviting them into the Garden; the same angelic encounter that closes delay for deniers in 16:33 becomes welcome for the faithful.
terra: The deniers are asked whether they await only the angels or their Lord's command; the repeated waiting formula places angelic arrival at the point when judgment ceases to be postponed.

terra: A witness is raised from every community and the disbelievers are neither permitted to answer nor allowed to seek favor; this supplies another community-by-community judicial assembly of witnesses.
terra: On the day a witness is raised in every community, the Prophet is وَجِئْنَا بِكَ as witness; this repeats the section's “bring, make present” action within testimony.

luna: On the day each soul comes pleading for itself and is repaid for what it did, arrival leads directly to personal accounting. It complements the section’s arrival scene with what that encounter requires of each person.

luna: The section’s secondary dictionary form of ف ج ر describes calamities bursting over a people; here opponents demand that a spring be made to burst from the earth. This is a concrete counter-sense of the root, continued by the demand for rivers in 17:91.

luna: The demand is for rivers to gush through a garden, using the section’s root ف ج ر in a provision scene rather than its dictionary image of sudden calamity; 17:90 gives the preceding spring demand.

terra: The challenger demands that God and the angels be brought قَبِيلًا, face-to-face, among proposed signs; the section answers that imagined spectacle with a final encounter the challenger does not control.

luna: The mountains are moved, the earth is seen bare, and all are gathered; 18:48 then presents them before their Lord in a row. This links the cleared ground to the human formation that follows. | terra: The mountains are removed, the earth appears bare, and all people are gathered without one being omitted; it prepares the exposed ground and complete assembly that the next verse arranges in a rank.

luna: The people are presented before their Lord in one row, صَفًّا; this is the human counterpart to the section’s repeated rows of arriving angels. | terra: Humanity is presented to the Lord صَفًّا and is told that it has come as first created; the verse joins the section's straight rank, divine presentation, and root ج ي ء in one judgment scene.

terra: The record is set down, the guilty see its contents, and everyone finds what they did present; the verse gives judicial content to the section's definition of bringing as making something present.

luna: The criminals see the Fire and know they are about to fall into it, finding no escape. This gives the section’s exposed Hell a specific human response: recognition that its appearance means their unavoidable destination. | terra: The guilty see the Fire, become certain that they will fall into it, and find no escape; visible recognition of the once-future destination directly develops the section's brought-into-view Hell.
terra: When the Lord's promise comes, the barrier is made دَكَّاءَ; the verse joins the root's leveling force to the arrival of a promised event, a compact parallel to the section's sequence.

luna: After the barrier opens, people surge over one another, يَمُوجُ فِي بَعْضٍ, as the trumpet is blown and all are gathered. This is the section’s dictionary root د ك ك crowding image in a final-day scene, with chaotic waves as a contrast to ordered rows; 18:100 then displays Hell. | terra: Immediately after the promised leveling of the barrier, people surge into one another, the trumpet is blown, and all are gathered together; the verse directly realizes the source dictionary's secondary image of a crowd pressing together and links it to the display of Hell in 18:100.

luna: Hell is displayed to the disbelievers on that day. Its being set before them parallels the section’s brought-forward Hell, while 18:99 supplies the preceding trumpet and gathering. | terra: God says Hell will be presented to the disbelievers عَرْضًا; the emphatic presentation is a direct nonlexical equivalent of bringing Hell before them.

terra: The deniers and devils are gathered and then made present around Hell kneeling; the verse reverses the section's motion while preserving its core relation—people and Hell are brought into one visible scene.

terra: Every person must come to or pass by Hell under a settled decree; following the gathering around it in 19:68, this makes the encounter universal while leaving the precise manner of arrival unstated.

luna: Each person will come to the Merciful on Resurrection Day alone, فَرْدًا. This individual arrival is a specific counter-image to the section’s collective rows of angels. | terra: Every one of creation comes to the Merciful on resurrection day individually; the solitary arrival sets a boundary on reading “rank after rank” as collective responsibility.

luna: Moses’ opponents are told to come صفًّا, in line, for the contest. The same physical formation stages a human confrontation, a boundary showing that a row by itself does not mean the section’s final assembly.
terra: Asked about the mountains, the speaker is told to say that his Lord will scatter them completely; this supplies the removal that produces the level, rank-ready plain described in 20:106-107.

luna: The mountains are blown away and the land left a level plain, قَاعًا صَفْصَفًا; 20:107 completes the picture by saying there is no crookedness or elevation on it. It gives the flattened stage preceding the section’s rows. | terra: After the mountains are scattered, the land is left قَاعًا صَفْصَفًا, a bare level plain; the root-shaped word and the leveled terrain make the ground itself fit the section's straight ranks.
terra: No crookedness or unevenness can be seen in the leveled land; it states the geometric condition that makes the section's “straight line” definition of صَفّ perceptible.

luna: People follow the Caller on that Day with no deviation, and their voices are humbled; 20:107 describes the level plain they cross. The verse adds directed, orderly movement toward a summons beside the section’s arrival in rows. | terra: Across the level plain everyone follows the caller without deviation and voices fall before the Merciful; it gives the straightened ground an equally directed human movement and a stance before God.

terra: The threatened event comes suddenly, confounds the deniers, cannot be repelled, and grants no respite; it closely matches the source dictionary's sudden onset of calamity, though no crowd or rank appears.

luna: Gog and Magog are released and rush down from every elevation; this gives the section’s dictionary sense of د ك ك as a crowd surging over something a distinct end-time mass movement, chaotic rather than in ranks. | terra: When Gog and Magog are released they rush down from every elevation; this is a concrete many-sided surge immediately before 21:97 announces the nearness of the true promise.

terra: When the true promise draws near, the disbelievers' eyes stare fixedly and they acknowledge heedlessness; nearness and sight reproduce the section's movement from remote warning to visible reality.

luna: The section’s dictionary form تَتْرَى means “one after another”; here messengers are sent in succession, and each community’s denial is followed by the next until they become tales. This makes the section’s repeated sequence concrete. | terra: Messengers are sent تَتْرَا, each nation denies its messenger, and the nations are made to follow one another into stories; this is the section's cited “one after another” sense and also explains its earlier peoples as a sequence.

terra: Birds are described as صَافَّاتٍ while all creation glorifies God; the root again marks an extended ordered posture, but here it most likely denotes spread wings rather than beings arranged in an eschatological line.

terra: The Fire sees the deniers مِن مَّكَانٍ بَعِيدٍ and they hear its rage; distance remains explicit here, yet the threat is already perceptible, clarifying the distance that the section's bringing finally abolishes.
terra: Those who do not expect the meeting demand that angels be sent to them or that they see their Lord; it supplies the defiant request whose answer the section's arrival scene embodies.

luna: When wrongdoers see the angels, the verse says there is no good news for them that day; 25:25 continues with the sky splitting and angels descending. It supplies the fearful human side of the angelic appearance in the section. | terra: The day the criminals finally see the angels brings them no glad tidings; it corrects the demand in 25:21 by showing that angelic visibility can mark exclusion rather than proof offered on their terms.

luna: On the day the sky splits with clouds, angels are sent down in a descent. Their arrival continues the section’s end-time scene, though this verse does not say they stand in rows. | terra: The sky splits with cloud and the angels are sent down in a great descent; this is the section's cited celestial opening through which the angelic company arrives.

luna: The verse lists ʿĀd, Thamud, the people of al-Rass, and many generations between them. This is another explicit chain of communities like the section’s remembered sequence of ʿĀd, Thamud, and Pharaoh.
terra: Immediately before Hell is exposed, the Garden is brought near to the God-fearing; the paired movement shows that final disclosure makes reward present as well as punishment.

luna: Hell is exposed to the misguided, وَبُرِّزَتِ الْجَحِيمُ لِلْغَاوِينَ; its own context identifies who faces the revelation that the section depicts. | terra: Hell is بُرِّزَتِ for the strayers; the same object in the section is made openly present, now with its audience identified.
luna: A rain is poured on Lot’s people and described as a terrible rain for those warned. This repeats the section’s specific image of sudden calamity descending on a people.

terra: A witness is drawn from every community and each people is challenged to produce its proof; this parallels the brought prophets and witnesses in the section's cited judgment scene, though the verb of bringing is different.

luna: At the trumpet, people emerge from their graves hastening to their Lord. This is another collective movement toward the Lord, though the verse pictures haste rather than the section’s ordered rows. | terra: At the trumpet blast people emerge from their graves and hurry toward their Lord; this contributes the mass arrival that precedes everyone being made present before God in 36:53.

luna: A single blast brings everyone before God; 36:51 gives the preceding emergence from graves. This provides a compact parallel to the section’s arrival and presentation scene. | terra: One cry leaves everyone جَمِيعٌ before God, made present; it condenses the section's successive spectacle into the instantaneous completion of the whole assembly.
terra: The demonstrative “This is Hell which you were promised” identifies the once-future object as immediately present; the pointing speech is what the section's bringing of Hell makes possible.

luna: The oath by الصَّافَّاتِ صَفًّا invokes beings arranged in ranks; it supplies another explicit image of the ordered formation named in the section. | terra: The oath وَٱلصَّافَّاتِ صَفًّا stages beings drawn into a rank with the same root and emphatic cognate form as the section; the verse itself leaves their identity implicit, so the spatial correspondence is firmer than the identification.

luna: Each angel says it has a known station, مَقَامٌ مَعْلُومٌ; the next verse, 37:165, identifies them as standing in ranks. The row’s own station detail develops the section’s dictionary form المَصَفّ, “standing-place.” | terra: The angelic speakers say that each has a known station, مَقَامٌ مَعْلُومٌ; this gives individual placement within the next verse's collective rank and concretizes the source section's definition of maṣaff as a standing-place.

luna: The angels say they are الصَّافُّونَ, “those in ranks,” directly naming the arrangement in the section. The preceding 37:164 adds that each has a known station, clarifying the standing-place sense of the section’s dictionary form المَصَفّ. | terra: The speakers say وَإِنَّا لَنَحْنُ ٱلصَّافُّونَ, identifying themselves by their act of forming ranks; this supplies an angelic first-person counterpart to the ranks that arrive in the section.
luna: This list names Noah’s people, ʿĀd, and Pharaoh before the next verse names Thamud and other factions. Its own contribution is to repeat the section’s sequence of named earlier communities.
luna: Thamud, Lot’s people, and the dwellers of the thicket continue the preceding list of earlier factions in 38:12; Thamud directly overlaps the section’s succession of punished peoples.
terra: After the first trumpet all collapse, and after the second they stand looking; this establishes the restored, seeing assembly into which the prophets and witnesses are brought in 39:69.

luna: Prophets and witnesses are brought, وَجِيءَ بِالنَّبِيِّينَ وَالشُّهَدَاءِ, for judgment; this is a concrete instance of the section’s dictionary sense of bringing something into presence. | terra: The transformed earth shines, the record is set down, and prophets and witnesses are وَجِيءَ بِـ them; this directly parallels Hell being brought into the judicial scene as something made present.

luna: Disbelievers are driven to Hell in groups, زُمَرًا: the section brings Hell to the scene, while this verse reverses the direction and brings the people to it. | terra: Those who disbelieved are driven to Hell in groups; instead of Hell being brought to humanity, humanity moves toward it, while the grouped procession preserves the section's distributive rhythm.

luna: The God-fearing are likewise led in groups to the Garden; this same judgment procession shows the other destination alongside the section’s brought-forward Hell. | terra: Those mindful of their Lord are driven to the Garden in groups; this repeats the grouped final procession but reverses its destination and reception.

luna: Angels encircle the Throne at the judgment’s conclusion, praising God as judgment is passed. This places an angelic assembly in the same final scene, though its circular arrangement differs from the section’s rows. | terra: After judgment the angels are seen surrounding the Throne and glorifying their Lord; the encircling placement gives another ordered angelic geometry around divine sovereignty, though it is not called a row.

terra: On the day all come forth, nothing about them is hidden from God and sovereignty is declared His alone; exposed humanity before the sovereign Lord parallels the section's fully assembled scene.

terra: Pharaoh's people are exposed to the Fire morning and evening, then ordered into the severest punishment when the Hour rises; this distinguishes repeated pre-Hour exposure from the section's once-for-all final presentation.
terra: God promises support on the day the witnesses stand; their taking their positions complements the section's cited scene in which witnesses are brought before judgment.

terra: God's enemies are gathered toward the Fire and يُوزَعُونَ, their ranks held together so the later ones catch the earlier ones; this is an ordered human procession toward Hell rather than an undifferentiated crowd.

terra: Angels descend upon the steadfast telling them not to fear or grieve and giving news of the Garden; this is the reassuring counterpart to the criminal's joyless sight of angels and to the section's judgment arrival.
terra: The condemned are seen exposed to the Fire, humbled and looking furtively; the verse makes both the presented punishment and the altered act of seeing concrete.
terra: The deniers are asked whether they await only the Hour coming suddenly while they are unaware; the verse repeats both the section's waiting stance and its dictionary image of abrupt calamity.

terra: The disbelievers are exposed to the Fire and told that they exhausted their good things in worldly life; the direction is reversed from the section—people are presented to Hell—yet the confrontation is equally visible.
terra: When the disbelievers are exposed to the Fire they are asked, “Is this not real?”; presenting them to what they denied supplies the reciprocal form of bringing Hell before them.
terra: The verse asks whether they await only the Hour coming suddenly, when its signs have already arrived; it is another direct formulation of expected judgment becoming an abrupt arrival.

luna: The people of Noah, the companions of al-Rass, and Thamud are named as earlier deniers; 50:13 continues the chain with ʿĀd and Pharaoh. Its own list repeats two peoples in the section’s historical sequence.

luna: This verse names ʿĀd, Pharaoh, and Lot’s people among those before; 50:12 precedes it with Noah’s people and Thamud, and 50:14 concludes that these groups denied messengers and the threat came true. It repeats the section’s succession of former peoples.

luna: The verse says the people of the thicket and Tubbaʿ denied the messengers, so the threat came true; 50:12–13 supply the preceding series, including Thamud, ʿĀd, and Pharaoh. It completes a parallel chain of rejected communities and judgment.

luna: Every soul comes accompanied by a driver and a witness, سَائِقٌ وَشَهِيدٌ. This gives the section’s general arrival a personal form, with each person escorted and attested. | terra: Every soul وَجَاءَتْ with a driver and a witness; the singular procession shows how the section's vast ordered arrival reaches each individual person.
terra: The heedless person's covering is removed and sight becomes sharp; after each soul arrives with driver and witness, this explains the new capacity to perceive what had been veiled.

terra: After each soul arrives with its driver and witness, a companion presents what is ready at hand; this adds an act of producing prepared evidence to the section's sense of making something present.

luna: Paradise is brought near to the God-fearing, a favorable counterpart to the section’s Hell brought into view; the verse makes the opposed destinations visible in the same judgment setting. | terra: The Garden is brought near to the God-fearing غَيْرَ بَعِيدٍ, “not far”; its explicit cancellation of distance is the positive counterpart to Hell being brought into view.

luna: The earth splits from the dead and they emerge rapidly; gathering them is described as easy for God. This gives the section’s incoming assembly another explicit emergence toward divine judgment.

terra: People are violently driven toward the Fire of Hell immediately before it is identified as the fire they denied; this verse contributes the forced motion into the confrontation stated in 52:14.
terra: “This is the Fire which you used to deny” names the object directly to those driven toward it; the demonstrative turns remembered denial into present encounter.
terra: Those leaving the graves are likened to scattered locusts; the swarm gives a concrete opposite to the straight angelic ranks while belonging to the same final assembly.

luna: People hasten toward the Caller, and 54:7 pictures them emerging from graves like scattered locusts. This is a judgment crowd moving toward a summons, with a dispersed form that contrasts with the section’s rows. | terra: After emerging like scattered locusts, they hurry toward the caller and name it a hard day; this gives the apparently disordered multitude in 54:7 a single direction and destination.

terra: In the Flood the earth is burst into springs and its water meets the descending water for a decreed matter; the root's literal mass outpouring explains the force behind the section's “calamities burst upon them” sense.
terra: “This is Hell which the criminals denied” changes denial into confrontation with a present object; it states the recognition produced by the section's exposed fire.

luna: The earth is violently shaken; 56:5–6 continue with mountains crumbling into scattered dust. This is another explicit earth-breaking scene beside the section’s pounding of the ground. | terra: The earth is shaken with a violent shaking; it begins another final dismantling of the ground that the section describes through pounding and leveling.
terra: The mountains are pulverized completely; this continues the loss of stable terrain that permits no surviving earthly height beside the section's flattened earth.
terra: The pulverized mountains become scattered dust; the verse completes the physical result of the preceding shaking rather than merely naming another judgment event.

terra: God sends messengers following in the predecessors' footsteps and then sends Jesus after them; the repeated following makes prophetic history another ordered succession rather than isolated arrivals.

terra: God “came upon them” from where they did not reckon and cast terror into their hearts; this use of coming for an unforeseen effective judgment marks a semantic boundary against imagining the section only as ordinary locomotion.

luna: Believers fighting in God’s cause are loved when they stand in a row, صَفًّا, like a solid structure. This gives the section’s straight-line formation a specific earthly counterpart. | terra: Those who fight in God's way صَفًّا are likened to a compact structure; the human battle line makes explicit the cohesion and straightness carried by the section's rank.
terra: The Fire is guarded by stern angels who never disobey God and perform every command; this joins angels and Hell in one ordered administration, though it does not describe ranks or an arrival.

terra: Birds above people are صَافَّاتٍ and then fold their wings; the same root pictures an extended ordered posture overhead, but the precise sense is wing-spreading rather than an eschatological rank.
terra: When the promised punishment is seen زُلْفَةً, brought close, the disbelievers' faces darken; the verse turns a disputed future threat into immediate sight just as the section does with Hell.

luna: This passage names Thamud and ʿĀd as denying the overwhelming event; 69:5–10 then recount their destruction and other punished peoples. It echoes the section’s sequence of past communities before its final scene.

luna: Thamud are destroyed by the overwhelming calamity; 69:4 names them with ʿĀd, and 69:6–10 extend the chain of punished peoples. This connects the section’s named sequence with another account of successive judgment.
luna: ʿĀd are struck by a furious wind, followed in 69:7 by seven nights and eight days of it; the account continues the sequence of earlier punished peoples recalled in the section.

luna: The wind against ʿĀd continues for seven nights and eight days, حُسُومًا; 69:8 asks whether any remnant remains. Its consecutive duration echoes the section’s interest in what comes one after another, within a specific destruction narrative.
luna: After the preceding wind against ʿĀd, the verse asks whether any remnant can be seen. This supplies the aftermath of the successive communal destructions recalled in the section.
luna: Pharaoh, those before him, and the overturned cities are named as further communities in error; 69:10 gives their seizure. The list parallels the section’s sequence that includes Pharaoh.
luna: They disobey their Lord’s messenger and are seized; 69:9 names Pharaoh and the overturned cities. This gives the punishment behind the sequence of communities recalled in the section.

luna: A single trumpet blast begins the sequence in which 69:14 says earth and mountains are crushed together; it supplies the event’s onset before the section’s flattened ground and rows. | terra: A single trumpet blast initiates the passage in which earth and mountains are crushed and the angels take their positions; the verse contributes the decisive summons that sets the whole ordered scene in motion.

luna: The earth and mountains are carried and crushed with one crushing, فَدُكَّتَا دَكَّةً وَاحِدَةً. This directly parallels the section’s dictionary root د ك ك for pounding the ground before the rows arrive. | terra: Earth and mountains are crushed دَكَّةً وَاحِدَةً; this is the closest lexical counterpart to the section's doubled pounding of the earth and begins the same scene that places the angels at heaven's edges.

luna: The sky is split open on that day, and 69:17 places the angels at its edges. The cited verse’s torn sky is the setting that completes the section’s arrival scene. | terra: Heaven splits and becomes frail immediately before the angel occupies its edges; this contributes the opened setting into which the section's ordered angelic presence expands.

luna: Here the singular collective الْمَلَكُ stands at the sky’s edges as it splits, matching the section’s note that الْمَلَكُ can name the whole angelic class and placing the rows in a larger judgment scene. | terra: The section explicitly pairs its collective singular وَٱلْمَلَكُ with this verse's وَٱلْمَلَكُ عَلَىٰ أَرْجَائِهَا; here the angels occupy the torn sky's edges and eight bear the Throne, giving the ranked arrival a wider spatial frame.
terra: On that day all are presented and no hidden thing remains hidden; following the crushed earth and positioned angels, the verse states the purpose of the assembled scene.
terra: The threatened event is something the deniers see as بَعِيدًا; this supplies the mistaken distance from which the section's brought-near spectacle begins.
terra: God sees the same event as قَرِيبًا; paired with the preceding human estimate, it explains why the apparently remote can suddenly stand present.
terra: The mountains become like wool in the passage that contrasts the deniers' distant estimate with God's nearness; physical dissolution is thus part of the event they mistakenly regard as remote.

luna: People rush from their graves toward a caller like scattered locusts; this is a specific mass-arrival scene whose scattering contrasts with the section’s ordered lines. | terra: People emerge rapidly from the graves as though racing toward a fixed marker; their directed convergence is a human analogue to a crowd pressing toward one point, without stating a straight rank.

luna: The earth and mountains shake, and the mountains become heaps of moving sand. This is a specific companion image of the final earth’s upheaval, though it does not itself show the rows. | terra: Earth and mountains quake and the mountains become a collapsing heap of sand; this is a material parallel to the section's crushed, leveled ground, though it does not stage the ranks.

terra: “Over it are nineteen” places the root ع ش ر in a count attached to Hell; the next verse identifies the counted guardians as angels, creating a concrete meeting of the section's ten-root, angels, and Fire.

terra: The guardians of the Fire are declared to be angels and their number a trial; this completes 74:30's counted scene and shows angelic order attached to Hell rather than only to the Lord's ranks.

terra: The oath invokes those sent forth عُرْفًا, often understood as being dispatched successively; that succession could echo the section's “one after another,” but the verse does not itself identify the agents or state a row.
terra: The mountains are blown away among the signs of the appointed day; their removal supplies another specific route from the existing landscape to the section's leveled ground.

luna: When the trumpet is blown, people come in groups, أَفْوَاجًا. It parallels the section’s repeated arrival, but groups are not the straight, repeated lines described there. | terra: At the trumpet blast people come أَفْوَاجًا, in crowds; the same surah later places Spirit and angels in one rank, distinguishing the human waves of arrival from the ordered heavenly line.
terra: The mountains are moved until they become a mirage; within the same surah as the arriving human crowds and standing angelic rank, this verse removes the old topography from their setting.

luna: The Spirit and angels stand صَفًّا on the Day of Judgment. Their fixed assembly extends the section’s image from arrival to the ordered gathering, under the verse’s rule that speech requires permission. | terra: The Spirit and the angels stand صَفًّا on the Day when speech requires permission; it directly realizes the section's angelic rank as an ordered standing before the Lord.
terra: The overwhelming catastrophe جَاءَتْ; a named final calamity itself “comes,” concretizing the section's broad coming verb and its dictionary image of calamities arriving suddenly.

luna: Hell is exposed to whoever sees it, وَبُرِّزَتِ الْجَحِيمُ لِمَن يَرَىٰ. This specifies the section’s bringing of Hell as a disclosure into sight. | terra: Hell is بُرِّزَتِ for everyone who sees; this directly states the section's claim that what seemed remote is exposed to sight.
terra: The deafening blast جَاءَتْ and immediately fractures family bonds; it is another final event whose coming makes an inescapable scene suddenly present.
terra: The mountains are set in motion during the upheaval that later kindles Hell and brings the Garden near; this contributes the destabilized terrain to that presentation scene.

terra: Hell is set blazing in the final sequence, immediately before the Garden is brought near; the pair shows punishment and reward made perceptible together, with this verse supplying the section's object.
terra: In the final upheaval the Garden is brought near; the same act of making a destination present carries promise here rather than the section's threat.

terra: On the last day the seas are فُجِّرَتْ, burst open; this gives an actual eschatological eruption to the source dictionary's figurative image of numerous calamities suddenly bursting upon people.
terra: Humanity stands before the Lord of the worlds; this supplies the eschatological standing-place implicit in the section's definition of maṣaff, though no linear arrangement is stated.

luna: The earth is stretched out and empties what is within it in 84:4; this is a related preparation of the final ground, though stretching and emptying are not the section’s pounding or rows. | terra: The earth is stretched out at the final upheaval; its extension corresponds to the section's prepared level expanse without using the pounding image.
terra: Human beings pass طَبَقًا عَن طَبَقٍ, stage after stage; the successive construction is a temporal analogue to the section's spatial “rank after rank.”

luna: The earth is shaken with its great earthquake, and 99:2 continues by having it cast out its burdens. The sequence gives the section’s ground-pounding a parallel in the upheaval before the earth’s final disclosure.
terra: People issue forth أَشْتَاتًا, as separate groups, to be shown their deeds; this scattered distribution is a human counter-image to the angels' straight ranks, while both serve disclosure.

luna: On that day people are like scattered moths. This same judgment crowd is pictured as dispersed, a concrete visual boundary to the section’s rows. | terra: People become like scattered moths on that day; their disordered movement sharpens the deliberate order of the section's angelic row after row.

terra: The mountains become like fluffed wool beside the verse's scattered human moths; their loss of solidity complements the section's crushed ground while continuing the same disorderly counter-image.
terra: The hearers are told they will surely see Hell; direct sight is the promised outcome of the section's act of bringing the unseen fire forward.
terra: The repeated promise specifies that Hell will be seen عَيْنَ ٱلْيَقِينِ; this gives the section's “before the eyes” claim its strongest epistemic form.
